chapter: Music in the family, learning to play
title: Child prodigy on piano: snare drum, lessons, Philip Gordon, Ida Flatricu
summary: Hirsch started on piano from his sister's lessons, loved drums, played for Philip Gordon, and studied at Newcomb paid for by his grandmother.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: So how did you get started playing? Me?

That's a long story. I was a child prodigy on the piano. I started, my sister was taking piano lessons. My mother, let me say this, my mother was a very fine pianist and a violinist. And my father was a very good trumpet player, a good cornet player. And there was always music in our house. And I used to like to play the snare drum. I like drums. And my daddy didn't want me to play drums. The only thing good about a drummer is that you're the first one on the job and the last one to leave and you better have a truck.

It's getting worse today. That's right. It's getting worse today. You'll see Ray Franson go on a job. I used to tell Ray, all I need is a bass drum and a snare drum. Oh, I have to bring the other equipment with me. And he sets up like this. So I have a snare drum bought from Grunewalds, Mr. Eckert. Old man Eckert. I think he sold every musician in town his first instrument. And my daddy bought me a snare drum. And he wouldn't buy me a set of drums. So my sister was studying piano. And I started looking at her books. And I'm reading her books and I'm reading before she's out of book one, I'm in book three. So the teacher heard me playing one day when she came to teach my sister. And she told my mother, she says, as long as I'm here, she says, I could teach your son too. She was paying 50 cents a lesson for my sister. And she says, I'm going to charge you two bits of lessons from Godfrey. I got a grand lesson for two bits. And I did very well. I played before Philip Gordon, who was a, after I started playing pretty good, I played before him. And he was a guy that used to make the roles for the Aeolian piano. The grand one. They started with the Aeolian roles for the grand pianos. In fact, he gave a concert and I was at the concert. And he was giving a demonstration to how you could, it was so realistic that you wouldn't know if it was a role or the artist playing on the thing. And after the concert, we were talking and talking and I said, well, I'll never be a good piano player. And I said, because my hands are so small. He said, let me see your hands. He said, look at mine. These are not much larger than yours. So that doesn't make any difference, small hands or large hands. It helps a little, but it doesn't hurt. So then Ida Flatricu, who was a teacher at Newcomb College, took me as a special student. I used to go up there on Saturdays. My father couldn't afford to pay for it. My grandmother, the mayor, she paid for it. She used to send my mother $5 a week for me. She charged me $5 a lesson, which was very, very expensive in those days. And I studied with Ida for quite a while until I lived across the street from a park and they were playing baseball and football. And here I am playing . So I wanted to play ball and then I wanted to play drums. And my uncle was in town and he bought me a bass drum and a couple of the things that go on it. And I went with Vic, did you know, do you remember Vic Pellegrini? Did you ever hear of Vic Pellegrini? I've heard the name. Vic Pellegrini, I don't remember his father's name but I think his father's name was Vic Pellegrini too.
